title: A fragment: the lost manuscript and the transcript
short: The poem begins in mid-sentence; its opening and ending were already lost when it was copied, and the manuscript itself burned in 1731.
body: The poem survives only because someone copied it before the Cotton Library fire at Ashburnham House in 1731, which destroyed its manuscript, Cotton Otho A.xii. That transcript, made around 1724, was printed by Thomas Hearne in 1726 in his edition of John of Glastonbury's chronicle. It was later found in the Bodleian Library (MS Rawlinson B. 203) in the 1930s. The copy has traditionally been credited to David Casley, the library's deputy keeper, though some scholars give it to John Elphinstone. Its text already lacked a beginning and an end, so it opens with the words 'brocen wurde' ('... should be broken'). Its 325 lines are the editors' numbering. Some of the odd spellings in this text (e.g. 'frymdi', 'wordon', 'hælæð') may be a later transcriber's misreadings of Anglo-Saxon letters, not the original scribe's forms. That is why many emendations are proposed.

title: The historical battle of 991
short: Byrhtnoth, ealdorman of Essex, was killed fighting a Viking army near Maldon in August 991; the English then began paying tribute.
body: The battle is a recorded event. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (versions C, D and E, s.a. 991) says Ipswich was harried and 'very soon after' ealdorman Byrhtnoth was killed at Maldon. It adds that in that year tribute was first paid to the Danes, 10,000 pounds, on the advice of Archbishop Sigeric. Version A, under 993 (a misdating), names the leader Anlaf and gives a fleet of ninety-three ships; some take him to be Olaf Tryggvason. Byrhtferth of Ramsey's Life of St Oswald, written soon after, makes Byrhtnoth a tall, white-haired religious hero. The twelfth-century Liber Eliensis says the Danes carried off his head and that he was buried at Ely; when his bones were found there in 1769 the skull was missing. Later monastic calendars date his death to 10 or 11 August. The poem was therefore written soon after the battle, or within a generation, but how soon is disputed.

title: The hawk let fly to the wood
short: Offa's young kinsman lets his beloved hawk fly to the wood: he gives up the aristocratic pastime of hunting for battle.
body: The cniht ('young man, youth') is a kinsman of Offa (l. 5). When he sees that the earl will not put up with cowardice ('yrhðo', l. 6), he releases his 'leofne' (dear) hawk towards the wood and goes to the fight. The poet spells out what it means: from this one 'could know' (oncnawan) that he would not weaken in the battle. Hawking was a sport of the nobility, and releasing the bird is a small, concrete act that marks the move from peaceful aristocratic life to deadly earnest. Critics often see it as a deliberate image of renunciation, done once and for good. It is one of the poem's few images drawn from daily life. The verb 'wacian' (l. 10, 'to weaken, grow slack') foreshadows the cowards later in the poem.

title: beot: the vow fulfilled
short: Eadric fulfils his beot, the formal vow of loyalty a retainer makes to his lord; the poem measures every man by this standard.
body: Old English 'beot' (Bosworth-Toller: vow, promise, also boast or threat) is the public pledge a warrior makes, often in the hall over mead, to do great deeds for his lord. It is not mere bragging: the vow binds the speaker. Eadric 'gelæste' (fulfilled, carried out) his vow when he had to fight before his lord. The poem is built on the contrast between vows kept and vows broken. Compare Ælfwine's reminder of what was said 'æt meodo' (l. 212), Offa's earlier warning that many boast who will not endure (ll. 198-201), and Offa's own vow (ll. 289-93). The messenger's speech is called 'on beot' (l. 27), a threat; the two senses of the word sit close together.

title: wicinga ar: the Viking messenger
short: A Viking herald calls out from the shore, offering peace in return for tribute; the poem gives the Viking army no named leader.
body: 'Ar' here means messenger or herald (compare 'ærende', errand, l. 28). He stands 'on stæðe' (on the shore, bank) and speaks 'on beot', threateningly. The Vikings are never named individually; they are 'brimliþendra' (seafarers, genitive plural, l. 27), 'sæmen' (l. 29), 'flotan' (l. 72), and 'wælwulfas' (l. 96). This anonymity contrasts with the English, whose names and kin are listed with care. The scene sets up a formal exchange of speeches across the water, with a challenge and a reply, before any fighting starts, as in heroic tradition.

title: gafol: tribute
short: The messenger demands gafol (tribute) in exchange for peace: the very policy the English adopted in 991.
body: 'Gafol' means tax, rent or tribute (Bosworth-Toller). The messenger proposes that the English 'buy off' (forgyldon) this spear-rush ('garræs') with tribute and rings ('beagas wið gebeorge', rings in return for protection). He speaks in a mercantile, almost legal language of deals: 'we willað wið þam golde grið fæstnian' (we will fasten a truce in exchange for the gold). The irony for the first audience was sharp. The Chronicle records that in 991 the English began paying tribute to the Danes, 10,000 pounds, the start of what was later called Danegeld. Byrhtnoth throws the word back in his reply: 'Hi willað eow to gafole garas syllan' (l. 46).

title: grið: a Norse loanword for 'truce'
short: 'Grið' (truce, protection) is a loan from Old Norse, perhaps a deliberate touch of Viking speech in the messenger's mouth.
body: Old English 'grið' comes from Old Norse 'grið' (truce, peace, sanctuary). It was a legal term that spread into late Old English law codes through Scandinavian settlement. The native word for peace in the next lines is 'frið' (ll. 39, 41). Several critics think the poet gives the messenger a few Norse or legalistic forms on purpose, so that his speech sounds foreign and calculating. Others caution that 'grið' was already established in English by the late tenth century. 'On hyra sylfra dom' (l. 38) means 'on their own terms, at their own judgement'. It is a legal phrase for a settlement whose terms are set by one side alone.

title: Byrhtnoth's reply: the speech formula
short: The heroic speech formula 'X maþelode' with ritual gestures (raising the shield, shaking the spear) introduces Byrhtnoth's defiant reply.
body: 'Maþelian' (to speak formally, make a speech) is a verb of poetry only; 'X maþelode' is the classic way a heroic speech begins, as often in Beowulf. Byrhtnoth lifts his shield and shakes his slender ash-spear ('wand wacne æsc'). He is 'yrre and anræd' (angry and resolute). The same formula and gestures come back in Byrhtwold's final speech (ll. 309-10), so the poem's two great speeches frame the battle. In his reply Byrhtnoth answers the messenger point by point. He takes up the messenger's own words (gafol, sceattas, scip, gangan) and turns them into weapons. Critics have long admired the speech as a piece of controlled scorn.

title: heregeatu: war-gear and heriot
short: 'Heregeatu' means war-gear but also 'heriot', the arms a dead man's heir returned to his lord: Byrhtnoth's tribute is a grim pun.
body: Bosworth-Toller gives 'military equipment' and also 'heriot'. A heriot was the payment of weapons, horses and money that a nobleman's heirs owed his lord at his death; late Anglo-Saxon wills record such heriots. Byrhtnoth says the English will pay tribute in spears, deadly points and old swords, 'that heriot which will not profit you in battle'. Many editors see a pun. The Vikings will receive weapons, but point first, and the 'heriot' will be paid on their own deaths. The word sums up Byrhtnoth's method of turning the messenger's commercial language into the language of war.

title: Æthelred's land
short: Byrhtnoth defends 'the land of Æthelred, my lord': Æthelred II, king 978-1016, later called 'the Unready'.
body: Byrhtnoth calls himself an 'unforcuð eorl' (an earl without reproach, l. 51) who will defend ('gealgean') this homeland ('eþel'). He names it as the land of Æthelred, 'ealdres mines' (my lord). The king is Æthelred II, whose reign saw renewed Viking attacks from the 980s and the tribute payments that began after Maldon. His later nickname 'Unræd' ('ill-counselled') puns on his name ('noble counsel'). The poem names him three times (ll. 53, 151, 203), always as the lord whom Byrhtnoth serves. The chain of loyalty in the poem runs from God through the king and the earl down to the retainers. 'Folc and foldan' (people and land, l. 54) is an alliterating pair typical of verse.

title: Pante: the River Blackwater
short: The Pante is the old name of the River Blackwater in Essex; the Vikings are camped on an island in its tidal estuary below Maldon.
body: The two armies face each other across the tidal water of the Pante, which is the Blackwater estuary; the upper river is still called the Pant. When the tide comes in ('flod æfter ebban', l. 65), the 'lagustreamas' (sea-currents) 'lucon' (locked together, closed in) round the island, so neither side can reach the other except with arrows. E. D. Laborde (1925) identified the Viking base as Northey Island, joined to the mainland at low tide by a causeway. That causeway is the 'bricg' of l. 74. Geological work by George and Susan Petty (1976) supported the identification, though other sites have been proposed. The topography in the poem is precise enough to make this identification widely accepted.

title: bricg: the causeway
short: 'Bricg' is the causeway to the island; Wulfstan, Ælfhere and Maccus hold it, so the Vikings cannot cross.
body: The 'bricg' is not a built bridge but the causeway exposed at low tide. Byrhtnoth, the 'hæleða hleo' (protector of warriors, a common formula), sets Wulfstan, son of Ceola, to hold it. Wulfstan kills the first man who steps onto it with his 'franca' (a spear or javelin, perhaps Frankish in origin). He is joined by Ælfhere and Maccus. Because three men can hold the narrow way, the Vikings cannot force a crossing. That leaves them only the trick of asking to be let across (l. 86), and so the poem explains why Byrhtnoth's decision at l. 89 matters so much.

title: Ælfhere and Maccus
short: Maccus is a non-English name, probably Scandinavian or Gaelic: a reminder that men of Danelaw descent fought on the English side.
body: The defenders of the causeway include Maccus, whose name is not Old English. It is usually explained as Norse or Gaelic (related to forms like Magnus or Gaelic Maccus) and is found in the Danelaw and the Irish Sea world. With Æscferth the Northumbrian hostage (ll. 265-67) and Ælfwine the Mercian (ll. 217-18), Maccus shows that Byrhtnoth's force drew on more than the men of Essex. The poem's cast of named English fighters is unusually long, and many critics think the poet named real men known to his audience. Few of them can be traced in other records.

title: lytegian: to act with guile
short: The Vikings, finding the causeway too well guarded, 'began to use guile' and asked to be allowed across.
body: Bosworth-Toller glosses 'lytigian' as 'to act cunningly', citing this line. The 'laðe gystas' (hateful guests) find that the 'bricgweardas' (guardians of the causeway) are fierce, so they ask that they may have 'upgang' (passage up, a landing) and bring their foot-soldiers ('feþan') across the ford. The word puts the blame for what follows on Viking cunning as well as on Byrhtnoth's response. The phrase 'laðe gystas' is ironic, since guests should be welcomed, and the poem reverses the duties of hospitality throughout.

title: ofermod: Byrhtnoth's pride
short: The most debated word in the poem: Byrhtnoth lets the Vikings cross 'because of his ofermod', which may mean pride or excessive courage.
body: Literally 'over-mind, over-spirit', 'ofermod' is glossed by Bosworth-Toller as 'pride, arrogance, over-confidence', and Latin 'superbia'. Elsewhere in Old English it describes Lucifer's pride (e.g. in Genesis B). Tolkien (1953) read the line as the poet's judgement: Byrhtnoth's chivalrous wish for a fair fight sacrificed his men, and the poem honours their loyalty while blaming his rashness. Gneuss (1976) showed that the word is pejorative in all its other uses, and since then 'pride' has been the dominant reading. Others still defend Byrhtnoth. They argue that 'ofermod' can be a heroic 'great spirit', or that a commander had good reason to bring on a battle rather than let the fleet sail off to raid elsewhere. Scholars still disagree on whether the poem condemns him, admires him, or does both.

title: landes to fela: too much land
short: Byrhtnoth 'allowed too much land to the hateful people': the poet's own verdict, phrased as an understatement.
body: 'Alyfan' means to allow, grant; 'landes to fela' (too much of land, partitive genitive) refers to the ground the Vikings were allowed to cross and the space to form up on the English side. The phrase is a rare direct comment from the narrator, and its 'to' (too) carries the judgement. Read with 'ofermod', it suggests that Byrhtnoth's generosity was a fault. Some critics hear a further irony: the earl who refused to give the Vikings gold gives them land instead, the very 'eþel' he swore to defend (l. 52). 'Laþere ðeode' means 'to the hateful people', the dative of 'lað' (hateful).

title: God alone knows who will hold the field
short: To 'control the place of slaughter' (wælstowe wealdan) is the standard Old English idiom for victory; Byrhtnoth leaves the outcome to God.
body: 'Wælstow' is the battlefield, literally 'slaughter-place'. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle repeatedly says the winners 'ahton wælstowe geweald' (had control of the field). Byrhtnoth's words that God alone knows who will hold it are pious, and they also show that he thinks the outcome is still open. Critics who blame him read the line as presumption, since he has thrown away a winning defensive position and left the result to chance. Those who defend him see trust in God. The same 'wælstowe' returns in Offa's vow (l. 293), where the place of slaughter has become the place of his death.

title: wihaga: the battle-hedge
short: 'Wihaga' (from wig-haga, 'war-hedge') is the shield-wall Byrhtnoth orders his men to form with their shields.
body: Bosworth-Toller gives 'wíg-haga', 'a phalanx', citing this line. The compound joins 'wig' (war) with 'haga' (hedge, fence, enclosure, as in 'haw'). Shields set rim to rim make a living fence. The poem uses several terms for this formation: 'bordweall' (l. 277) and 'scyldburh' (shield-fortress, l. 242). Its breaking is the military result of Godric's flight. 'Feohte neh, tir æt getohte' (battle was near, glory in the fight, ll. 103-04) puts the start of the fighting in a pair of half-lines that echo each other.

title: The beasts of battle
short: Ravens circle and the eagle is eager for carrion: the traditional 'beasts of battle' theme that marks the start of slaughter.
body: Old English poets often bring in the raven, the eagle and the wolf when battle is about to begin, waiting for corpses. Magoun (1955) called this a recurring 'theme' of oral-formulaic composition; it occurs in Judith, Exodus, Elene, Brunanburh and elsewhere. Here the 'earn æses georn' (eagle eager for carrion) and wheeling 'hremmas' (ravens) appear with the outcry ('hream') of the armies. Maldon uses the theme briefly, as a single image, before the poet turns to the spear-throwing. The wolf is present only in the Vikings themselves, the 'wælwulfas' of l. 96.

title: Sister's son
short: Wulfmær, Byrhtnoth's sister's son, is the first named English casualty: in Germanic tradition the bond with a sister's son was especially close.
body: Tacitus (Germania 20) remarks that among the Germans a sister's son was held in the same honour by his uncle as by his father. The idea recurs in Old English heroic poetry (Beowulf and Hygelac; the Finnsburh story). The poet underlines the relationship ('Byrhtnoðes mæg ... his swuster sunu'), and the next line reports at once that 'wiþerlean' (requital) was given to the Vikings. The pattern of kinship, death and vengeance prepares for the second half of the poem, where vengeance for Byrhtnoth himself becomes the only aim. This Wulfmær should not be confused with Wulfmær 'se geonga', son of Wulfstan (l. 155).

title: suþerne gar: the southern spear
short: The Viking throws a 'southern spear' at Byrhtnoth: whether it means a spear made in the south, or thrown from the south, is unclear.
body: 'Suþerne' means 'southern'. Editors have taken it in different ways. It may mean a spear of southern make, perhaps Frankish, from the Rhineland weapon trade, like the 'franca' of ll. 77 and 140. Or it may be a spear of English make from the Viking's northern point of view, or simply a conventional epithet. It is one of several unexplained details in the duel. Byrhtnoth pushes the shaft away with his shield so that it breaks, and then kills two men in turn. The 'særinc' (sea-warrior) here and 'ceorl' (l. 132), a term for a man of lower rank, keep the Viking anonymous and socially below the earl.

title: Byrhtnoth laughs
short: Having killed his assailants, Byrhtnoth laughs and thanks God for his day's work: heroic laughter joined with Christian thanksgiving.
body: 'Modi' (spirited, brave, also proud; related to 'mod') describes Byrhtnoth as he laughs and thanks the Lord ('metod', the measurer, a poetic name for God) for the 'dægweorc' (day's work) that God has granted him. Laughter in battle is a heroic gesture, found also in Old Norse literature. The thanksgiving makes the warrior's labour a gift from God. The moment is brief: at once a 'dreng' throws a dart that pierces him (ll. 149-51). Critics read the laughter in opposite ways, either as admirable courage or, in the light of 'ofermod', as another sign of the earl's over-confidence.

title: Wulfmær the young
short: Wulfmær son of Wulfstan, a 'hyse unweaxen' (a youth not yet full-grown), avenges his lord by returning the Viking's own spear.
body: The poet takes care to describe him as young: 'hyse unweaxen' (an ungrown youth), 'cniht on gecampe' (a boy in the battle). He acts 'full caflice' (very boldly). His father is probably the Wulfstan who held the causeway (l. 75). His deed prepares for the general theme of revenge in the second half. It also sets up the contrast of youth and age running through the poem: the hawk-flying 'cniht' (l. 9), the 'har hilderinc' Byrhtnoth (l. 169), Ælfwine 'wintrum geong' (l. 210), and the old retainer Byrhtwold (l. 310).

title: har hilderinc: the grey-haired warrior
short: Disarmed and wounded, the grey-haired Byrhtnoth still urges his men forward: 'har' marks his age, confirmed by other sources.
body: When a Viking cripples his sword-arm, Byrhtnoth's 'fealohilte swurd' (sword with yellowish, i.e. gold-coloured, hilt) falls to the ground. He can no longer hold his 'heardne mece' (hard blade; 'mece' is a poetic word for sword). Still 'har hilderinc' (grey battle-warrior), he encourages his men. Byrhtferth's Life of St Oswald says he had white hair, and he had been ealdorman since 956, so he was probably over sixty. His age adds pathos and links him with Byrhtwold, the 'eald geneat' who speaks the poem's most famous lines. The half-line 'hyssas bylde' (encouraged the young men) fixes his last act as a leader.

title: Byrhtnoth's dying prayer
short: Byrhtnoth thanks God and prays that his soul may pass to Him in peace and not be harmed by 'hell-foes', the devils.
body: The prayer echoes the Christian commendation of the soul at death. He thanks the 'ðeoda waldend' (ruler of peoples) for the joys of his life. He asks the 'milde metod' (gentle Creator) to grant his spirit good, so that his soul may journey ('siðian') into God's keeping, and that the 'helsceaðan' (hell-ravagers, demons) may not harm ('hynan') it. In medieval belief the soul at death could be contested by angels and devils, and the 'þeoden engla' (prince of angels) is asked to protect it. The speech has a hagiographic quality. Some critics compare it to martyr narratives and to the dying Roland's prayer in the Chanson de Roland, while others point to the differences.

title: frymdi: entreating
short: 'Frymdi' is usually read as 'entreating, suppliant' ('I beseech you'); the form is odd and may be the transcriber's.
body: Bosworth-Toller enters 'frymdi', 'inquisitive, asking, desirous, suppliant', citing this very line. It relates it to 'frimdig' (desirous) found in Ælfric. 'Ic eom frymdi to þe' thus means 'I am asking of you, I entreat you' that the hell-foes may not harm my soul. The spelling without final -g is unusual, and editors debate whether it reflects late Essex speech, an error in the lost manuscript, or the transcript. Either way the sense is clear. The line ends the prayer in humble petition after the strong verbs of the heroic narrative.

title: Godric's flight on his lord's horse
short: Godric, son of Odda, flees first, leaping on Byrhtnoth's own horse and its trappings; his brothers Godwine and Godwig follow.
body: 'Hi bugon þa fram beaduwe þe þær beon noldon' (then those who did not wish to be there turned from battle) starts the movement of the cowards. Godric 'forlet' (abandoned) the good man who had often given him a 'mear' (horse), a typical lord's gift. He leapt on the 'eoh' (horse, a rare poetic word) that his lord owned, 'on þam gerædum þe hit riht ne wæs' (in the trappings, which was not right). The theft of the lord's horse makes the betrayal concrete and later deceives the army (ll. 239-42). The three brothers' names alliterate in G (Godric, Godwine, Godwig). The poet's narrating presence is sharp here: he comments on rightness and wrong.

title: Offa's warning at the assembly
short: Offa had warned at a council that day that many who spoke boldly would not stand firm in need; the warning comes true.
body: 'Meþelstede' (meeting place, place of speech) and 'gemot' (assembly) refer to a council held earlier on the day of the battle. There Offa observed that many spoke 'modiglice' (bravely, proudly) who would not endure 'æt þearfe' (in time of need). The passage looks back to a scene not in the surviving poem, perhaps once told in the lost opening. It confirms the poem's main moral test: the gap between words and deeds, between the 'beot' and its fulfilment. Offa himself, by contrast, keeps his vow (ll. 289-94).

title: To die or to avenge
short: The retainers resolve on one of two things: to give up their lives or to avenge their lord. Survival without vengeance is not an option.
body: The vow that a retainer should not leave the field alive when his lord has fallen is often traced to Tacitus (Germania 14), who says it was lifelong shame to survive one's chief in battle. Roberta Frank (1991) challenged this assumption. She argued that the ideal of dying with one's lord is rare in earlier Germanic and Old English literature, and that Maldon may reflect a late tenth-century literary fashion rather than ancient custom. Others reply that the motif appears in the Chronicle's Cynewulf and Cyneheard episode (s.a. 755). Either way, the speeches that follow all repeat this choice, each in the speaker's own voice.

title: Remembering the mead-hall vows
short: Ælfwine reminds his comrades of the vows made over mead on the hall benches: now it can be tested who is brave.
body: 'Mæl' (speech, saying) here means the formal vows ('beot', l. 213) that the warriors 'ahofon' (raised, made) 'on bence' in the hall 'æt meodo' (at the mead). The ideal of the mead-hall pledge, repaid in battle, is ancient in Germanic heroic verse. Compare Wiglaf's reproach to Beowulf's companions in Beowulf, which uses the same idea of drinking the lord's mead and failing him. 'Nu mæg cunnian hwa cene sy' (now can be tested who is keen) uses the subjunctive 'sy' for an open question. The test of vows is the poem's central theme.

title: Ælfwine and his Mercian ancestry
short: Ælfwine, son of Ælfric, boasts of his Mercian lineage: his grandfather Ealhelm was an ealdorman, and Byrhtnoth was both kinsman and lord.
body: Ælfwine, 'wiga wintrum geong' (a warrior young in winters), declares his 'æþelo' (noble descent). He is of a great family in Mercia ('on Myrcon'), and his grandfather Ealhelm was a 'wis ealdorman, woruldgesælig' (wise ealdorman, prosperous in the world). An ealdorman named Ealhelm is recorded in Mercia in the 940s. Historians have tentatively identified Ælfwine's father Ælfric with Ælfric 'cild', ealdorman of Mercia, exiled in 985, though this is uncertain. Ælfwine says no thegns among his people shall reproach him ('ætwitan') for going home lordless, because Byrhtnoth 'wæs ægðer min mæg and min hlaford' (was both my kinsman and my lord). Kin and lordship, the two great bonds of the heroic world, are joined in one man.

title: The army deceived by the horse
short: Offa explains the catastrophe: seeing Godric on Byrhtnoth's horse, many thought their lord was fleeing, and the shield-wall broke.
body: Offa's speech gives the military cause of the defeat. 'Formoni man' (very many a man) thought, when Godric rode off on the proud steed ('wlancan þam wicge'), that it was their lord. So the army ('folc') was split ('totwæmed') and the 'scyldburh' (shield-fortress) broken. Offa calls Godric 'earh' (cowardly, Bosworth-Toller: 'timorous, fleeing through fear') and curses his action: 'Abreoðe his angin' (may his undertaking fail, perish; optative subjunctive). Unlike the hawk scene, where the poet tells us what the action means, here the meaning comes from a character inside the poem.

title: Dunnere, the simple ceorl
short: Dunnere, a 'simple, humble' freeman, also calls for vengeance: loyalty is shown to be felt across ranks, not only by nobles.
body: Bosworth-Toller glosses 'unorne' as 'simple, plain, poor, humble'. A 'ceorl' was a free man of non-noble rank. That a ceorl shakes his dart and cries 'ofer eall' (over all) that no man may hesitate ('wandian') who means to avenge his lord shows the heroic ethic reaching down the social scale. Some critics take this as the poet's idealisation, others as a realistic note about the levy. Earlier the Viking who wounds Byrhtnoth is also called a 'ceorl' (l. 132), in contrast with 'eorl'. Dunnere's short speech is the plainest statement of the vengeance theme.

title: Æscferth the Northumbrian hostage
short: Æscferth, son of Ecglaf, a Northumbrian hostage, fights eagerly for his captors: a hostage's loyalty to the household that held him.
body: A 'gysel' was a hostage given as surety for the good conduct of his kin or people. Æscferth was perhaps a pledge from Northumbria, an area of strong Scandinavian settlement whose loyalty to the West Saxon king was uncertain. That he 'ne wandode na' (did not hesitate at all) but shot arrows ('flan') again and again shows that the household's bond could cover even an outsider. Critics often compare the Chronicle's Cynewulf and Cyneheard story (s.a. 755), where a hostage also fights. 'Hwilon ... hwilon' (sometimes ... sometimes, l. 270) gives his actions a steady rhythm.

title: cellod bord: an unexplained shield
short: 'Cellod' is found only in this phrase here and in the Finnsburh Fragment, and its sense is uncertain: perhaps 'keeled' or 'boat-shaped'; the corslet then 'sang a terrible song'.
body: Bosworth-Toller enters 'célod, céllod', from 'ceol' (keel of a ship), and glosses it Latin 'scaphiformis', 'boat-shaped'. Bosworth-Toller cites the same phrase, 'cellod bord', in the Finnsburh Fragment (l. 29), and editors have linked the two passages, though the sense remains uncertain. The word may describe a convex or curved shield. 'Bærst bordes lærig' (the rim of the shield burst) and 'seo byrne sang gryreleoða sum' (the mail-coat sang a song of terror) are a vivid personification, with the ringing of the iron rings turned into a dreadful song.

title: Offa's vow fulfilled
short: Offa had vowed that he and his lord would both ride home safe or both fall in battle; he dies 'thegnly' beside Byrhtnoth.
body: Offa kills a Viking 'sælida' (seafarer), then is cut down himself. The poet says he had accomplished ('geforþod') what he promised his 'beahgifa' (ring-giver, a kenning for lord). Either they would both ride 'on burh' (to the stronghold, home) unharmed ('hale to hame'), or both perish in the army ('on here crincgan') and die of wounds on the 'wælstow' (field of slaughter). 'He læg ðegenlice ðeodne gehende' (he lay like a thegn, close to his lord) is an epitaph in a single line. The alliteration on þ/ð binds 'thegn' and 'lord' together. His vow pairs with Offa's earlier warning (l. 198) and with the hawk of his young kinsman.

title: Byrhtwold, the old retainer
short: Byrhtwold, 'eald geneat' (an old retainer), speaks with the same formula and gestures as Byrhtnoth before the battle.
body: 'Geneat' (Bosworth-Toller: companion, associate, vassal) is the household companion; 'eald' marks long service. The introduction ('maþelode, bord hafenode ... æsc acwehte') repeats almost word for word the frame of Byrhtnoth's reply to the messenger (ll. 42-43). The echo matters: the last speaker takes the dead lord's place as the voice of the troop. Nothing else is known of Byrhtwold. The poem gives no patronymic for him, only age and loyalty. His speech, spoken 'ful baldlice' (very boldly), 'teaching' ('lærde') the warriors, is the moral climax of the poem as we have it.

title: 'Mind must be the harder'
short: The most famous lines in Old English heroic verse: resolve must grow as strength shrinks, set out in two balanced comparative clauses.
body: Grammar: 'sceal' (must, shall) governs each clause; 'þe heardra', 'þe cenre', 'þe mare' are comparatives preceded by the instrumental 'þe' ('the harder ... the keener'). These are answered by 'þe ure mægen lytlað' ('as [lit. by that which] our strength lessens'). The three key nouns, 'hige' (thought, courage), 'heorte' (heart) and 'mod' (mind, spirit), name the inner self, while 'mægen' (might, physical strength) is the outer power that fails. The lines alliterate on h and m. Critics have compared the sentiment to the Old Norse heroic poem Bjarkamál, known through Saxo Grammaticus. The lines are often quoted as a summary of the northern heroic spirit, the will that refuses defeat when defeat is certain, and Tolkien made them central to his reading. The irony that Byrhtnoth's 'ofermod' caused this situation has often been noted.

title: 'I am old in life'
short: Byrhtwold, old in years, will not leave: he means to lie beside his lord, 'so dear a man'. Loyalty is fulfilled in death.
body: 'Frod feores' (old in life; genitive of respect) recalls the 'frod fyrdrinc' Byrhtnoth (l. 140). 'Fram ic ne wille' (I will not [go] away) leaves the verb of motion unstated, a common Old English construction. He intends to lie 'be healfe' (by the side) of his lord. 'Licgan þence' (I mean to lie) makes death a deliberate choice. 'A mæg gnornian' (ever may he mourn, l. 315) curses anyone who thinks of turning from this 'wigplega' (war-play, a poetic compound for battle). Frank's argument (1991) that dying with one's lord is a new literary ideal applies above all to this passage. Critics who stress continuity with older tradition read it as the purest expression of the comitatus ethic.

title: The other Godric: the poem breaks off
short: A second Godric, son of Æthelgar, fights to the death; the poet insists he is not the Godric who fled, and there the transcript ends.
body: Godric son of Æthelgar ('æþelgares bearn') throws his 'wælspere' (slaughter-spear) at the Vikings and goes 'fyrmest' (foremost) until he falls ('gecranc'). The poet adds at once that this was not the Godric who 'ða guðe forbeah' (avoided the battle). The care to separate the two men suggests that the audience knew the names and that a son of Odda's disgrace was a real matter of reputation. It also shows how the poem uses names: identity and lineage decide honour and shame. The text ends here mid-passage, so we do not know how far the lost ending went or whether it followed the fight to the end.
